entries.title: The weight of a flower
entries.category: dictionary-labelled proverbial saying; editorial close reading
entries.literal_meaning: The queen cannot bear the weight of a flower.
entries.explanation: The joke makes an almost weightless thing into a burden fit to overwhelm a queen. The dictionary defines the flower-weight expression as the weight of something very light; it does not identify a queen or describe an actual incident. Our reading hears exaggerated delicacy in the contrast. In a playful exchange, it could tease someone who makes a tiny agreed task sound immense. That use depends on knowing the situation: the line cannot tell us whether another person is in pain or what they can safely manage.
entries.meaning_odia: ଫୁଲ ପରି ହାଲୁକା ଜିନିଷର ଭାର ବି ରାଣୀ ସହିପାରୁନାହାନ୍ତି—ଏହି ବଢ଼ାଇ କହିବାରେ ହସ ଅଛି। ଅଭିଧାନ “ଫୁଲର ଭର”କୁ ଅତି ହାଲୁକା ବସ୍ତୁର ଭାର ବୋଲି ବୁଝାଏ; କୌଣସି ନିର୍ଦ୍ଦିଷ୍ଟ ରାଣୀଙ୍କ ଘଟଣା ଦିଏନାହିଁ। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଅତି ସୁକୁମାର ଭାବ ଦେଖାଇବାର ଟାହି ଶୁଣାଯାଏ। ଆଗରୁ ରାଜି ହୋଇଥିବା ଛୋଟ କାମକୁ କେହି ବଡ଼ ବୋଝ କରି କହିଲେ, ସାଙ୍ଗମାନଙ୍କ ମଧ୍ୟରେ ଏହା ହାଲୁକା ଥଟ୍ଟା ହୋଇପାରେ। କିନ୍ତୁ କାହାର କଷ୍ଟ ବା ସାମର୍ଥ୍ୟକୁ ଏହି କଥାରୁ ମାପିହେବ ନାହିଁ।
entries.english_summary: A flower becomes an enormous burden in an exaggerated picture of delicacy.
entries.odia_summary: ଫୁଲର ହାଲୁକା ଭାରକୁ ଅସହ୍ୟ ବୋଝ କରି ଦେଖାଇବାରେ ଟାହି ଅଛି।
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: Two friends have agreed to put one sheet of labels on a noticeboard. One jokingly sighs that the work will take all day. The other answers with the flower-and-queen line, and they laugh before starting. This harmless teasing scene is an editorial application, not a collected performance.
entries.cultural_context: The queen is the figure named in the saying, not proof of a historical royal custom or a trait of women. No medical judgment or obligation to ignore discomfort is implied. The source gloss defines light weight, not a complete social-use rule.

entries.title: Affection and familiarity
entries.category: dictionary-labelled proverbial saying; editorial close reading
entries.literal_meaning: If you lavish affection on the dog, it licks your face.
entries.explanation: The response is close and physical: affection is answered by a lick on the face. The headword gloss specifies excessive fondness, which gives the image its edge. Our reading follows the speaker’s complaint that encouraged familiarity has become more intimate than expected. The joke can also turn back on that speaker: what kind of response did the invitation encourage? Applying it to people is a sharp comparison, not a neutral description of their worth; boundaries can be discussed without treating anyone as inferior.
entries.meaning_odia: ଗେହ୍ଲା ପାଇ କୁକୁର ମୁହଁ ଚାଟୁଛି—ଉତ୍ତରଟି ଅତି ନିକଟର। ଅଭିଧାନର ଶବ୍ଦାର୍ଥରେ ଅତ୍ୟଧିକ ଗେହ୍ଲା କରିବା ବା ମୁହଁ ଦେବା ଅଛି। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ, ନିଜେ ବଢ଼ାଇଥିବା ନିକଟତା ଆଶାଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ହେଲା ବୋଲି କହୁଥିବା ଲୋକର ଅଭିଯୋଗ ଶୁଣାଯାଏ। ହସଟି ତାଙ୍କ ଆଡ଼କୁ ମଧ୍ୟ ଫେରିପାରେ: ସେ ନିଜେ କେମିତି ଉତ୍ତରକୁ ଉତ୍ସାହ ଦେଇଥିଲେ? ମଣିଷକୁ ଏହି ତୁଳନାରେ କହିବା ତୀକ୍ଷ୍ଣ ଟାହି; କାହାକୁ ହୀନ କରିବା ଛଡ଼ା ମଧ୍ୟ ନିଜର ସୀମା କହିହୁଏ।
entries.english_summary: Our reading notices how encouraged familiarity can exceed the inviter’s expectations.
entries.odia_summary: ନିଜେ ବଢ଼ାଇଥିବା ନିକଟତା ନିଜ ଆଶାଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ହେବାର ଟାହି ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଆସେ।
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: A club organizer tells friends to drop in whenever they like, then complains when they arrive during his quiet afternoon. He quotes the dog line about his own overgenerous invitation. A friend suggests stating visiting hours clearly instead of blaming the guests. The self-directed use is an editorial choice.
entries.cultural_context: The dictionary marks the headword Sambalpur regional usage; that is not an exclusive origin claim. Quoted ଲାର୍ଡ is retained without silently changing it to the headword spelling ଲାଡ଼. This is a reading of a social comparison, not animal-care guidance or a rule that kindness produces ingratitude.

entries.odia: ଡାହାଣୀ ହୋଇ ଲାଗିବା; ଗୁଣିଆ ହେଇ ଝାଡିବା
entries.title: Creating trouble, claiming the cure
entries.category: dictionary-labelled proverbial saying; editorial close reading
entries.literal_meaning: To afflict as a witch, then drive it out as the healer.
entries.explanation: Two roles face one another in a short, balanced line: the one associated with the affliction and the one who removes it. The headword explains possession in the language of a historical belief. Our close reading treats the paired roles as an image of someone creating trouble and then claiming credit for relief. The change of role, rather than a documented supernatural event, supplies the sting. A modern example can expose a manufactured problem without making accusations of witchcraft against any person.
entries.meaning_odia: ଛୋଟ କଥାଟିରେ ଦୁଇ ଭୂମିକା ମୁହାଁମୁହିଁ—ଲାଗିବା ଭୂମିକା ଓ ଝାଡ଼ିବା ଭୂମିକା। ଅଭିଧାନର ଶବ୍ଦାର୍ଥରେ ଅପଦେବତା ଆବିର୍ଭାବର ପୁରୁଣା ବିଶ୍ୱାସ ଅଛି। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଏହି ଯୋଡ଼ି ଭୂମିକା ନିଜେ ଅସୁବିଧା ତିଆରି କରି ପୁଣି ତାହା ଦୂର କରିବାର ଶ୍ରେୟ ନେବାର ଚିତ୍ର ହୁଏ। ଭୂମିକା ବଦଳରେ କଥାର ଦଂଶନ ଅଛି; ଏହା କୌଣସି ଅଲୌକିକ ଘଟଣାର ପ୍ରମାଣ ନୁହେଁ। ଆଜିର ଉଦାହରଣରେ କୃତ୍ରିମ ସମସ୍ୟାକୁ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ କରିହୁଏ, କାହାକୁ ଡାହାଣୀ ବୋଲି ଅଭିଯୋଗ ନକରି।
entries.english_summary: Our reading sees the same person creating a problem and claiming credit for its remedy.
entries.odia_summary: ନିଜେ ସମସ୍ୟା କରି ତାହାର ସମାଧାନର ଶ୍ରେୟ ନେବାର ଚିତ୍ର ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ଆସେ।
entries.usage_example: Original imagined example: An organizer deliberately removes a useful instruction from a form, then presents restoring it as his special solution to everyone’s confusion. A colleague quotes the paired-role line while explaining what changed. The example criticizes the documented alteration, not anyone’s supposed supernatural powers.
entries.cultural_context: The supernatural vocabulary is historical source language, not an endorsed explanation of illness. The dictionary supplies the headword definition and saying, not an explicit figurative-use gloss; the manufactured-problem reading is editorial. No identified healer, ritual, community practice or origin is established.
